stem: A 54-year-old man with multiple sclerosis has painful extensor spasms and clonus in both legs. His neurologist prescribes an oral GABA analog that acts on a G-protein-coupled receptor in the spinal cord, and the spasms ease as excitatory input to his motor neurons falls.
oneliner: 54M + MS + extensor spasms + clonus + spinal metabotropic GABA agonist → which changes?
ask: Which set of changes at the spinal synapse follows activation of this receptor?

options.A: K+ efflux ↔, Ca2+ entry ↔, Cl- influx ↑, glutamate release ↔
options.B: K+ efflux ↓, Ca2+ entry ↑, Cl- influx ↔, glutamate release ↑
options.C: K+ efflux ↑, Ca2+ entry ↓, Cl- influx ↔, glutamate release ↓
options.D: K+ efflux ↔, Ca2+ entry ↓, Cl- influx ↔, glutamate release ↓
options.E: K+ efflux ↑, Ca2+ entry ↔, Cl- influx ↔, glutamate release ↔

whyNot.A: Chloride influx through a channel is the signature of the **ionotropic** receptor; this drug acts on a **G-protein-coupled** receptor
whyNot.B: Closing K+ channels and opening Ca2+ entry would **raise** transmitter release, but his spasms ease as **excitatory input falls**
whyNot.D: A G-protein-coupled inhibitory receptor signals through G-protein subunits that **open K+ channels**, so K+ efflux cannot stay unchanged
whyNot.E: Easing of spasms means **excitatory input to motor neurons falls**, so glutamate release cannot be unchanged

answer: K+ efflux up, presynaptic Ca2+ entry down, glutamate release down
why: A GABA-B agonist (baclofen) activates a **Gi/o-coupled** receptor: the G-protein subunits **open K+ channels** and **close presynaptic Ca2+ channels**. The neuron hyperpolarizes and **less glutamate is released** onto the motor neuron, which reduces spasticity.
chain: Drug binds a G-protein-coupled GABA receptor
G-protein subunits open K+ channels
Presynaptic Ca2+ channels close
Cell hyperpolarizes and glutamate release falls
Motor neuron drive and spasticity decrease

idea.rule: Gi/o-coupled inhibitory receptors open K+ channels and shut presynaptic Ca2+ channels, so cells hyperpolarize and release less transmitter.
also: Opioid mu receptors reduce presynaptic Ca2+ entry and open K+ channels
Muscarinic M2 receptors in the sinus node open K+ channels and slow the heart
Alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine lower norepinephrine release through Gi
Dopamine D2 receptors are Gi-coupled

stem: A 32-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has had 4 days of blurred vision in the right eye with a dull ache on eye movement. Both eyelids open fully, eye movements are full and the pupils are equal at 4 mm in room light. A light is shone into each eye in turn.
oneliner: 32F + MS + right blurred vision + ache on eye movement + equal pupils → which pupil responses?
ask: Which set of pupillary constriction responses fits her? (arrows show how well the pupil constricts)

options.A: Right eye lit: right ↓, left ↓; left eye lit: left ↔, right ↔
options.B: Right eye lit: right ↓, left ↔; left eye lit: left ↔, right ↓
options.C: Right eye lit: right ↔, left ↔; left eye lit: left ↓, right ↓
options.D: Right eye lit: right ↔, left ↓; left eye lit: left ↓, right ↔
options.E: Right eye lit: right ↔, left ↔; left eye lit: left ↔, right ↔

whyNot.B: This pattern is a **right efferent (CN III) lesion**: the right pupil would fail whichever eye is lit, but her pupils are **equal at rest** and the **lids and eye movements are normal**
whyNot.C: This is the mirror image: it needs an afferent lesion on the **left**, but her visual loss is in the **right** eye
whyNot.D: A left efferent lesion leaves the left pupil unreactive and would give **ptosis and a motor deficit**; she has full eye movements and open lids
whyNot.E: Normal responses cannot explain **visual loss confined to the right eye** with **pain on eye movement**, which point to an inflamed right optic nerve

answer: Reduced constriction of both pupils when the right eye is lit; normal when the left is lit
why: Optic neuritis damages the **afferent limb** from the right eye, so light there sends a weak signal to **both** Edinger-Westphal nuclei and **both pupils** constrict poorly. Light in the left eye gives a strong signal and **both constrict normally**. The efferent limb is intact, so the swinging flashlight test shows a relative afferent defect.
chain: Right optic nerve inflamed
Afferent signal from the right eye is weak
Both Edinger-Westphal nuclei get a weak drive
Both pupils constrict poorly when the right eye is lit
Left eye lit: afferent limb intact, both pupils constrict normally

idea.rule: An afferent lesion weakens the response of both pupils when the bad eye is lit; an efferent lesion silences one pupil whichever eye is lit.
also: Relative afferent pupillary defect: both pupils dilate as the light swings to the bad eye
CN III compression leaves the dilated pupil unreactive to light in either eye
Optic neuritis is a common first sign of multiple sclerosis
A severe retinal detachment also causes an afferent defect

stem: A 22-year-old man is admitted after a motorcycle crash. A penetrating wound over the right motor cortex has left his left leg completely paralyzed, and his right radial nerve was severed at the humerus. When casts are removed 10 weeks later, his reflexes and tone are examined.
oneliner: 22M + right cortical wound + paralyzed left leg + severed right radial nerve + 10 weeks → which reflexes?
ask: Which set of findings is expected at 10 weeks?

options.A: Left ankle jerk ↓, right brachioradialis jerk ↓, left leg tone ↓
options.B: Left ankle jerk ↔, right brachioradialis jerk ↓, left leg tone ↔
options.C: Left ankle jerk ↑, right brachioradialis jerk ↑, left leg tone ↑
options.D: Left ankle jerk ↑, right brachioradialis jerk ↓, left leg tone ↑
options.E: Left ankle jerk ↓, right brachioradialis jerk ↑, left leg tone ↓

whyNot.A: Low reflexes and tone belong to the **early shock phase** after an acute central lesion; by **10 weeks** the cord arc is released and the left leg has lost its cortical control
whyNot.B: The cortical wound removes **descending inhibition** of the left leg's arc, so its reflex and tone cannot stay normal
whyNot.C: The brachioradialis arc runs through the **severed radial nerve**, so that reflex cannot be brisk
whyNot.E: This swaps the sides: the **cortical** lesion affects the **left leg**, and the **cut nerve** is on the right arm

answer: Left ankle jerk and leg tone up, right brachioradialis jerk down
why: The stretch reflex arc (Ia afferent to alpha motor neuron) lives in the cord. The cortical lesion removes **descending inhibition**, so once the early flaccid phase passes the **left leg is spastic and hyperreflexic**. Cutting the **radial nerve** breaks the arc itself, so the **right brachioradialis jerk is lost**.
chain: Right motor cortex wound removes descending inhibition
Left leg arc is released once the early flaccid phase fades
Left ankle jerk and tone rise
Right radial nerve cut breaks its own arc
Right brachioradialis jerk is lost

idea.rule: A central lesion releases reflexes and raises tone; a peripheral nerve cut abolishes the reflex because the arc is broken.
also: Upper motor neuron lesion: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign
Lower motor neuron lesion: flaccid weakness, wasting, absent reflexes
Spinal cord transection: brisk reflexes and spasticity below the level once spinal shock resolves
A dorsal root or sensory nerve lesion also abolishes the reflex

stem: A 44-year-old woman dies after a 9-year illness of brief, irregular dance-like limb movements, a disjointed gait and progressive memory loss. Her father had a similar illness and died in his sixties. At autopsy her caudate and putamen are shrunken, and the substantia nigra looks normal. Transmitter levels are measured in the striatum.
oneliner: 44F + dance-like movements + dementia + affected father + small caudate, normal nigra → which striatal transmitters?
ask: Which set of striatal transmitter levels is expected?

whyNot.A: Low dopamine with relatively high acetylcholine is the pattern of **nigral cell loss**, but her **substantia nigra is normal**
whyNot.C: Isolated acetylcholine loss fits a cortical dementia; her **striatum is shrunken**, so striatal GABA neurons must be lost too
whyNot.D: GABA cannot rise when the **caudate and putamen are shrunken**, and dopamine is not lost with a normal nigra
whyNot.E: Her **nigra is normal**, so dopamine input to the striatum is intact; it is relatively **raised** because its target neurons are gone

answer: GABA down, acetylcholine down, dopamine relatively up
why: Huntington disease kills **medium spiny GABAergic neurons** and cholinergic interneurons of the caudate and putamen. The **nigrostriatal dopamine input is spared**, so dopamine is relatively increased and chorea results. Her earlier death than her father's fits **anticipation** from a CAG repeat expansion.
chain: CAG repeat expansion makes mutant huntingtin
Striatal GABAergic and cholinergic neurons die
GABA and acetylcholine fall
Nigrostriatal dopamine input is spared
Dopamine is relatively high and chorea appears

idea.rule: Huntington disease: striatal GABA and acetylcholine fall, dopamine is spared (relatively high); Parkinson disease is the opposite.
also: Autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4
Anticipation, especially with paternal transmission
Caudate atrophy enlarges the frontal horns on imaging
Parkinson disease: nigral dopamine loss with relative acetylcholine excess
Alzheimer disease: acetylcholine falls from nucleus basalis loss

stem: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes suddenly develops continuous flinging movements of the right limbs. Mental status and the rest of the examination are unremarkable. MRI shows a small lacunar infarct in the left subthalamic nucleus.
oneliner: 68F + diabetes + sudden flinging right arm and leg + left subthalamic lacune → which circuit changes?
ask: Which set of basal ganglia changes best explains her movements?

options.A: Subthalamic drive to GPi ↑, GPi inhibition of thalamus ↑, thalamocortical drive ↓
options.B: Subthalamic drive to GPi ↔, GPi inhibition of thalamus ↑, thalamocortical drive ↓
options.C: Subthalamic drive to GPi ↓, GPi inhibition of thalamus ↓, thalamocortical drive ↓
options.D: Subthalamic drive to GPi ↑, GPi inhibition of thalamus ↓, thalamocortical drive ↑
options.E: Subthalamic drive to GPi ↓, GPi inhibition of thalamus ↓, thalamocortical drive ↑

whyNot.A: More drive to GPi and more inhibition of the thalamus would **slow** movement; she has **excess** movement, and an infarcted nucleus cannot drive harder
whyNot.B: Increased pallidal inhibition suppresses movement, the opposite of her **continuous flinging**
whyNot.C: A drop in thalamocortical drive would give **too little** movement; with less GPi inhibition the thalamus is freed, not silenced
whyNot.D: The infarct destroys the **subthalamic nucleus**, so its drive to GPi cannot rise

answer: Subthalamic drive down, GPi inhibition of thalamus down, thalamocortical drive up
why: The glutamatergic **subthalamic nucleus excites GPi**, and GPi inhibits the thalamus. After a subthalamic infarct **GPi is less active**, so the thalamus is **disinhibited** and drives the motor cortex more. The result is contralateral flinging movements (hemiballismus).
chain: Left subthalamic nucleus infarcted
Excitation of GPi is lost
GPi inhibits the thalamus less
Thalamus drives motor cortex harder
Right-sided flinging movements

idea.rule: Subthalamic nucleus output is excitatory to GPi; losing it frees the thalamus and causes excess contralateral movement.
also: Lacunar infarcts from diabetes or hypertension are the usual cause
Parkinson disease has the opposite flow: more GPi inhibition, less movement
Direct pathway (D1) lowers GPi output and promotes movement
Indirect pathway (D2) raises GPi output via the subthalamic nucleus

stem: A 58-year-old man had a left upper lobectomy for lung cancer a year ago. He now has 2 months of hoarseness and dull left shoulder pain. Chest CT shows a recurrent mass at the left lung apex, and his left eye and face are examined.
oneliner: 58M + prior lung cancer resection + hoarseness + shoulder pain + left apical mass → which left eye and face changes?
ask: Which set of left-sided changes is expected?

options.A: Pupil size ↑, upper lid height ↓, facial sweating ↔, light reflex ↓
options.B: Pupil size ↓, upper lid height ↓, facial sweating ↑, light reflex ↔
options.C: Pupil size ↓, upper lid height ↓, facial sweating ↓, light reflex ↔
options.D: Pupil size ↔, upper lid height ↓, facial sweating ↔, light reflex ↔
options.E: Pupil size ↑, upper lid height ↑, facial sweating ↑, light reflex ↔

whyNot.A: A large, poorly reactive pupil is a **CN III** picture; an apical mass beside the **sympathetic chain** does not explain it, and sweating would be unaffected
whyNot.B: The sympathetic nerves are what stimulate facial sweat glands, and an apical mass **interrupts** them, so sweating cannot increase
whyNot.D: Isolated lid droop with normal pupil and sweating would suggest a levator problem; a **mass at the lung apex** damages the whole sympathetic supply
whyNot.E: Dilated pupil, retracted lid and excess sweating are **sympathetic overactivity**; the mass **destroys** that pathway

answer: Small pupil, drooping lid, less sweating, light reflex intact
why: A Pancoast-type mass at the lung apex interrupts the **oculosympathetic pathway** (ciliospinal center C8-T2, chain or plexus). Loss of the dilator pupillae gives **miosis**, loss of the superior tarsal muscle gives **mild ptosis**, and facial **sweating falls** on that side. The parasympathetic light reflex is untouched.
chain: Apical mass compresses the sympathetic chain
Dilator pupillae loses its drive
Pupil is small, light reflex still works
Superior tarsal muscle loses its drive, lid droops mildly
Sweat glands lose supply and sweating falls

idea.rule: Sympathetic loss to the eye gives a small, reactive pupil, mild ptosis and reduced facial sweating on the same side.
also: Pancoast tumor at the lung apex
Carotid dissection causes Horner syndrome with neck pain
Lateral medullary infarct causes ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Brachial plexus lower trunk injury can affect the same pathway
Cluster headache can cause a transient Horner pattern

stem: A 28-year-old man has a complete cervical spinal cord transection above the level of the sympathetic outflow after a rugby tackle. Two weeks later he develops pneumonia, and circulating pyrogenic cytokines reach his hypothalamus.
oneliner: 28M + complete high cervical transection + pneumonia → which response still occurs?
ask: Which response to the infection is still possible in this man?

options.B: A rise in the hypothalamic temperature set point

whyNot.A: Skin vasoconstriction depends on **sympathetic outflow**, which lies below the transection
whyNot.C: Shivering is driven by **descending pathways** from the hypothalamus, which the transection **cuts**
whyNot.D: Sweat glands are supplied by **sympathetic cholinergic fibers** below the lesion, which are cut off from the hypothalamus
whyNot.E: Brown fat heat production is **sympathetic (norepinephrine)** driven, and that outflow is disconnected from the hypothalamus

answer: Rise of the hypothalamic set point
why: Cytokines act on the hypothalamus to raise the set point through **prostaglandin E2**, and that structure sits **above** the lesion, so this step still happens. Every effector that must travel down the cord (**vasoconstriction, shivering, sweating, brown fat**) is lost below the transection.
chain: Cytokines raise PGE2 in the hypothalamus
Set point rises (above the lesion, so intact)
Descending signals to effectors are interrupted
Vasoconstriction, shivering, sweating and brown fat are lost

idea.rule: Fever is a hypothalamic event and still starts after high cord transection, but the effectors below the lesion cannot carry it out.
also: Aspirin lowers the set point by blocking prostaglandin synthesis
IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha induce hypothalamic COX-2 and PGE2 regardless of cord injury
Spinal cord transection patients are prone to poikilothermia
Hypothalamic damage rather than cord damage abolishes fever

stem: A 31-year-old man has a complete spinal cord transection at T1 after a fall from a ladder. In rehabilitation he asks in which situations he could still achieve and sustain an erection.
oneliner: 31M + complete T1 transection + asks about erections → which stimulus still works?
ask: Which of the following can still produce an erection?

whyNot.A: Psychogenic erection depends on **descending pathways** from the brain, which a T1 transection interrupts
whyNot.B: Dreams generate the signal in the **brain**, and the message cannot cross the **transection**
whyNot.C: Reading is a cortical stimulus that needs **descending input**, which is cut
whyNot.E: Testosterone supports libido but does not restore the **neural pathway**; the problem here is the transection, not hormone level

why: Touch to the penis triggers a **sacral reflex** (pudendal afferents to the S2-S4 parasympathetic pelvic nerves) that releases nitric oxide and fills the penis. That arc lies **below the transection**, so reflex erection persists. Psychogenic erections need descending signals and are lost.
chain: Complete cord transection above the sacral cord
Brain-origin signals cannot descend
Penile touch activates the S2-S4 reflex arc
Pelvic nerve releases nitric oxide
Erection occurs without brain input

idea.rule: Reflex erection uses the intact S2-S4 arc; psychogenic erection needs descending pathways and is lost after a high cord lesion.
also: Parasympathetic S2-S4 causes erection (point)
Sympathetic T11-L2 drives psychogenic erection and emission
Somatic pudendal nerve controls ejaculatory contraction (shoot)
Cauda equina lesions abolish reflex erection

stem: A 49-year-old woman is drowsy with a worsening headache 5 days after coiling of a ruptured berry aneurysm. CT shows no mass, and all four ventricles, including the fourth, are enlarged.
oneliner: 49F + ruptured aneurysm 5 days ago + drowsy + all four ventricles enlarged → what changed in CSF flow?
ask: Which set of CSF changes best explains the scan?

options.A: CSF production ↔, arachnoid villus absorption ↔, aqueductal flow ↓
options.B: CSF production ↑, arachnoid villus absorption ↔, aqueductal flow ↔
options.C: CSF production ↔, arachnoid villus absorption ↑, aqueductal flow ↔
options.D: CSF production ↓, arachnoid villus absorption ↓, aqueductal flow ↔
options.E: CSF production ↔, arachnoid villus absorption ↓, aqueductal flow ↔

whyNot.A: A blocked aqueduct would **leave the fourth ventricle small**, but hers is **enlarged** along with the others
whyNot.B: Overproduction needs a source such as a choroid plexus papilloma; **CT shows no mass**, and the recent **bleed** is the obvious change
whyNot.C: Greater absorption would **shrink** the ventricles, not enlarge them
whyNot.D: Nothing in the stem lowers **choroid plexus output**, and the recent **subarachnoid bleed** acts on absorption, not production

answer: CSF absorption down; production and aqueduct flow unchanged
why: Blood from the ruptured aneurysm **clogs the arachnoid villi**, so **absorption falls** while the choroid plexus keeps producing CSF at the same rate. With the aqueduct patent, fluid backs up and **all ventricles enlarge**: communicating hydrocephalus.
chain: Subarachnoid blood clogs arachnoid villi
Absorption of CSF falls
Production is unchanged
CSF accumulates and all four ventricles enlarge

idea.rule: Communicating hydrocephalus is failed absorption at the arachnoid villi; obstructive hydrocephalus is a block within the ventricular system.
also: Meningitis scarring the subarachnoid space or villi
Aqueductal stenosis enlarges lateral and third ventricles but spares the fourth
Choroid plexus papilloma causes overproduction
Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating form in older patients
